title: A Portrait for the Harvest
premise: Emrys Ravensworth, a reclusive pest controller who survives by being forgettable, is hired to clear vermin from his late grandmother's house and discovers photographs in which an extra chair appears in every frame after 1974. The chair belongs to his aunt Maren, who vanished that autumn, and the house's resident presence will not release the family until what was stolen from her—a locket buried in the well—comes back to light. As frost creeps through the walls spelling out accusations, Emrys uncovers that his own father helped bury the truth, and that the entity feeds on the silence of the guilty. In the end, Emrys publicly confesses the family crime at the harvest feast, returns the locket, and lets the house take him in Maren's place, finally seen by everyone.
about_author: Juniper Vane is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent a decade cataloguing abandoned farmsteads across the Welsh marches. Her debut novella, 'The Tally of Doors,' won a small-press horror prize and was praised for making domestic inventory feel like a séance.

chapters.title: The Man Who Keeps the Lights On
chapters.summary: Emrys Ravensworth, POV. We meet him mid-job, sealing a farmhouse against rats, establishing his rituals: lights on, doors counted, face forgotten. He takes a call to his late grandmother's house he didn't know he inherited. Beat: uneasy competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Vermin with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. At the house he finds droppings arranged in neat rows and a door scratched from the inside of a locked pantry. His professional logic cracks against evidence of something deliberate. Beat: the first wrongness—his tools are useless here.

chapters.title: Every Photograph, One More Chair
chapters.summary: Emrys POV, night. Sorting his grandmother's albums, he notices a plain wooden chair appearing in family photos after 1974, positioned where no one sits. The final album shows the chair facing the camera. Beat: dread of being watched by the past.

chapters.title: Maren, 1974
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Maren's diary entries interleaved with Emrys reading them. She recorded a harvest visitor no one else acknowledged and a locket she hid in the dry well. Beat: grief and curiosity fusing into obsession.

chapters.title: The Frost Begins to Spell
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Frost patterns on the windows form letters overnight: G-U-I-L-T, then his father's name, Aldous. Emrys calls his father, who goes silent and hangs up. Beat: the past reaches into the present; family trust fractures.

chapters.title: Aldous Comes Home
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Aldous arrives uninvited, demanding Emrys burn the house down. He confesses fragments: the harvest visitor was a debt collector for a crime Aldous committed, and Maren saw everything. Beat: love against duty—father begging son to stay blind.

chapters.title: The Well Gives Back
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. Against Aldous's pleas, Emrys descends the dry well and finds Maren's remains and the locket, along with a child's shoe that is his own. The house exhales; every door he counted stands open. Beat: horror that he was always part of it.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Maren's POV, finally fully voiced through the house. She reveals the harvest entity doesn't want the locket—it wants acknowledgment, a name spoken publicly. Aldous tries to flee with the locket and the frost takes his hands. Beat: justice outside the law arrives.

chapters.title: The Harvest Feast
chapters.summary: Emrys POV. He carries the locket to the village harvest gathering and confesses the 1974 crime aloud, naming Maren before the whole town. The entity's presence gathers behind him like weather. Beat: climax—choosing truth over the family's survival.

chapters.title: A Portrait, Finished
chapters.summary: Village POV, after. The house stands empty but warm; in every photograph of that final harvest, Emrys sits in the extra chair beside Maren, both smiling. A new pest controller is called to something with fingerprints, and the lights stay on. Beat: resolution—the price of survival paid, and peace found in being finally seen.
